title: Trace Repeated Claims Back to Their Underlying Sources
subtitle: Check whether several pages are independent or are repeating the same origin.
description: When several pages or reports repeat the same claim, follow their links and citations back to the underlying material, record shared documents, datasets or organizations, and distinguish independent origins from repeated summaries.

lifeOsSource.hack: When several pages repeat the same claim, trace each one back far enough to see whether the underlying material is actually independent or shared.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the claim, list the pages or reports repeating it, follow their citations or links toward the origin, note shared documents, datasets, organizations or copied wording, and classify the set as independent origins, shared origin, mixed, or unclear.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which items looked separate, what underlying origin did each one use, where did they overlap, and how many genuinely distinct origins remain?

faq.question: Do different websites count as independent sources?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Two websites can repeat the same announcement, document, dataset or earlier article. Follow the attribution chain far enough to identify what each page actually relies on.

faq.question: What if I cannot reach the original material?
faq.answer: Mark the lineage as unclear. You can still record which intermediate sources are shared, but do not turn an unresolved chain into a claim of independence.
faq.answerHtml: Mark the lineage as unclear. You can still record which intermediate sources are shared, but do not turn an unresolved chain into a claim of independence.

faq.question: Does a shared source make the claim wrong?
faq.answer: No. This protocol only prevents repeated publication from being counted as multiple independent origins. Whether the underlying claim is correct requires a separate evaluation of the material itself.

intro.html: Seeing the same statement in several places can create the appearance of several independent confirmations even when the pages trace back to one origin. Source lineage separates repetition from independence: follow the chain, record shared origins, and count distinct underlying material rather than distinct browser tabs.

sections.title: 1. Freeze the repeated claim
sections.html: Write the specific statement that appears across the items. Keep wording close enough that you can tell whether the pages are truly making the same claim or only discussing the same topic.

sections.title: 2. Trace each item toward its origin
sections.html: Follow citations, links, named documents, announcements, datasets and attributed quotations. Stop when you can identify the material that the item actually depends on, or when the chain becomes unavailable.

sections.title: 3. Mark shared lineage
sections.html: Record when multiple items rely on the same underlying document, dataset, organization, author group, announcement or copied wording. Also note mixed cases where the items share one origin but add genuinely separate material.

sections.title: 4. Classify independence explicitly
sections.html: Label the set as independent origins, shared origin, mixed, or unclear. Use that classification when summarizing what you found so repeated summaries do not silently become additional independent support.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported claims about repetition, judgment improvement and training targets, fabricated tracing outcomes, rigid timing rules and high-stakes examples with a bounded source-lineage procedure.
